sec: Bilirubin excretion · urobilinogen, LFT fractions and disease taxonomy

items.q: Following bacterial degradation in the colon, what respective proportions of urobilinogen undergo fecal clearance as stercobilinogen versus re-entry into the portal blood?
opts: 80% excreted in feces and 20% reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation
50% excreted in feces and 50% reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation
95% excreted in feces and 5% reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation
60% excreted in feces and 40% reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation
items.exp: Of the deconjugated urobilinogen, 80% is excreted in feces as stercobilinogen, while 20% enters the enterohepatic circulation back to the liver. (Book p987)

items.q: Fill up: Bacterial degradation and deconjugation of bilirubin diglucuronide into urobilinogen occurs predominantly at the ______ and colon.
items.exp: The flowchart specifies that degradation by colonic bacteria occurs at the ileocecal junction and colon. (Book p987)

items.q: Match each clinical state with the corresponding urinary urobilinogen finding — 1) Normal healthy individual 2) Extravascular hemolysis 3) Complete biliary tract obstruction … A) High urinary urobilinogen B) Absent urinary urobilinogen C) Traces of urinary urobilinogen
items.exp: Normal urine contains traces of urobilinogen; extravascular hemolysis produces high urobilinogen; and biliary tract obstruction causes complete absence of urinary urobilinogen. (Book p987)

items.q: A 54-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis exhibits increased urobilinogen in her urine despite having normal red blood cell turnover. What is the pathological mechanism responsible for this finding?
opts: Failure of cirrhotic hepatocytes to take up reabsorbed enterohepatic urobilinogen, causing systemic spillover
Increased bacterial deconjugation in the terminal ileum secondary to gut dysbiosis
Hyperactivation of renal tubular urobilinogen secretory transporters
Accelerated intravascular clearance of delta bilirubin into the urine
items.exp: In cirrhosis with functional defects, reabsorbed enterohepatic urobilinogen is not taken up by the liver and escapes into the systemic circulation, filtering into urine. (Book p987)

items.q: Assess the two statements on hemolysis: I Extravascular hemolysis typically produces high urinary urobilinogen without hemoglobinuria. II Intravascular hemolysis is characterised by hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria.
items.exp: Both statements are true: extravascular hemolysis yields elevated urobilinogen, whereas intravascular hemolysis results in free hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria. (Book p987)

items.q: What are the reference numerical thresholds for total, indirect, and direct bilirubin on an automated panel?
opts: Total: 1–1.3 mg/dL; indirect: 0.2–0.9 mg/dL; direct: 0–0.3 mg/dL
Total: 0.1–0.5 mg/dL; indirect: 0.05–0.2 mg/dL; direct: 0.2–0.5 mg/dL
Total: 2.0–3.5 mg/dL; indirect: 1.5–2.5 mg/dL; direct: 0.5–1.0 mg/dL
Total: 0.5–2.0 mg/dL; indirect: 0.1–0.4 mg/dL; direct: 0.4–1.6 mg/dL
items.exp: Normal bilirubin values are Total: 1–1.3 mg/dL, Unconjugated/indirect: 0.2–0.9 mg/dL, and Conjugated/direct: 0–0.3 mg/dL. (Book p987)

items.q: Which analytical technique is specified for the accurate estimation of serum bilirubin fractions?
items.exp: The note explicitly states that bilirubin fractions are estimated by HPLC (High-performance liquid chromatography). (Book p987)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six standard parameters listed under Liver Function Test (LFT) on this page?
items.exp: The six LFT parameters listed across the header branch are Bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, Serum Albumin, and Serum Globulin; GGT is discussed later under cholestasis markers. (Book p987)

items.q: Match each broad category of liver disease with its typical target or progression — 1) Hepatic parenchymal disorder 2) Cirrhosis end-stage consequence … A) Sinusoidal and hepatocyte involvement progressing from acute to chronic hepatitis B) Portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and functional liver failure
items.exp: Hepatic parenchymal disorders involve the sinusoids/hepatocytes and can progress to cirrhosis, which subsequently leads to portal HTN, HCC, and functional liver failure. (Book p987)

items.q: Fill up: The brown pigment in stool formed by the oxidation of deconjugated intestinal urobilinogen is ______.
items.exp: Eighty percent of deconjugated intestinal urobilinogen is excreted in feces as stercobilinogen. (Book p987)

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with deep jaundice, pale clay-coloured stools, and dark tea-coloured urine. A dipstick examination of the urine reveals conjugated bilirubin but zero urobilinogen. What is the most likely site of disease?
opts: Isolated defect in canalicular MRP-3 transporter
items.exp: Complete biliary tract obstruction blocks conjugated bilirubin from entering the gut lumen, completely abolishing urobilinogen formation and urinary urobilinogen. (Book p987)

items.q: Assess the two statements on liver disease classification: I Liver diseases are classified into hepatic parenchymal, vascular, and biliary disorders. II Hepatic parenchymal disorders progress directly to hepatocellular carcinoma without passing through cirrhosis.
items.exp: Statement I is true. Statement II is false because the flowchart depicts acute hepatitis progressing to chronic hepatitis, then to cirrhosis, which subsequently leads to HCC, portal HTN, or liver failure. (Book p987)
